subject: religious-studies
title: Irenaeus, Hick, and Soul-Making
welcome_lead: Walk into the second-century church of Lyons and then forward to Birmingham, where John Hick reads Irenaeus afresh.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on the Irenaean theodicy and Hick's soul-making.
final_note: Soul-making does not erase suffering but offers a vision in which it can be transfigured.

concepts.def: Irenaeus' view that humans are made first in the 'image' of God and must grow into the 'likeness' through moral struggle.
John Hick's term for the developmental process by which souls become virtuous through engagement with evil and suffering.
Hick's idea that a degree of separation from direct knowledge of God is necessary for genuine freedom and faith.
Hick's view that the soul-making process will eventually be completed for all persons, perhaps beyond death.
The claim that present sufferings can only be justified in the light of a final consummation.
The phrase Hick borrows from John Keats' 1819 letter, in which life is 'a vale of soul-making'.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130-202), in Against Heresies, distinguishes between the 'image' (capacity) and 'likeness' (realised holiness) of God in humanity.

Adam was created spiritually immature, and the trajectory of salvation history is the maturation of humanity in Christ, the new Adam, through whom we are 'recapitulated'.

John Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966) reworks Irenaeus for the modern era. God creates humans at an 'epistemic distance' so that we may freely choose to grow into His likeness.

Suffering is the necessary context for the cultivation of virtues like courage, patience, and compassion; a 'paradise' world would be morally meaningless.

Hick recognises that not all soul-making is completed in this life. He therefore embraces universalism: the process continues post-mortem until all souls reach their telos.

Critics argue this trivialises present moral choices and that some sufferings (e.g. dysteleological evils, the Holocaust) cannot be redeemed even eschatologically.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.

Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.

options: If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.

Substance dualism means men and women are different.

options: Substance dualism is the belief that humans have two personalities.
Substance dualism means men and women are different.
